learningObjectives: Explain how models can support multiple software lifecycle work products
Identify benefits of model-based development for consistency, simulation, formal verification and code generation
Recognize risks where models fail to express robustness, architecture, basic software or operating-system aspects
Describe back-to-back testing and verification models
concept: Use models across requirements, architecture, unit design, implementation, integration and verification while controlling risks from incomplete modelling, code generation, resource usage, and model-code equivalence.
Model-based development can affect more than one software lifecycle work product, including requirements, architectural design, detailed design, integration and generated code.
Models can capture functionality, behavior, design or properties of software and support requirements verification and validation by simulation or formal methods.

Models can support architectural design by describing static aspects such as components, interfaces, data flows and attributes, and dynamic aspects such as event chains, scheduling and message passing.

Executable code can be generated directly from models; this can lower manual coding error risk but may introduce issues if robustness properties, resource use, generated-code verifiability or model-code equivalence are not controlled.
Verification models can support back-to-back testing, early fault detection, efficient test generation, automated testing and formal verification.
whyItMatters: Model-based development can improve lifecycle continuity and consistency but can also concentrate systematic faults if model scope and tool behavior are misunderstood.
Safety evidence must cover both the model and generated code, including robustness and target-resource behavior.
activities: Use models to capture requirements, architecture or unit design
Generate code from qualified model artefacts where applicable
Analyze resource usage of generated code
Document textual explanations for aspects not captured by the model
automotiveExample: A chassis-control algorithm is designed in Simulink, verified by MIL and SIL tests, auto-generated to C, back-to-back tested against the model, and checked for execution time and memory consumption on the target ECU.
commonMistakes: Assuming a model captures all safety requirements
Omitting textual requirements for robustness against missing or erroneous inputs
Ignoring basic software and operating-system architecture outside the model
Underestimating resource usage of generated code
